sections.heading: Zero-Knowledge Proof of Seed: Architecture and Motivation
sections.summary: zkBoo proofs running on stock Ledger Flex prove HD wallet key ownership without exposing secrets, enabling emergency quantum-break recovery via account abstraction.
sections.body:
- The project is an emergency mitigation for an unexpected quantum break, based on Vitalik's 2024 proof-lifting proposal.
  - Key desiderata: must work on today's hardware wallets, must not require user pre-action before an emergency, and must not force users to relinquish security.
- The approach lifts ECDSA to a quantum-resistant scheme by proving knowledge of a hard-to-invert pre-image in the HD wallet key derivation chain, then delegating authority on-chain via account abstraction.
- Focus is on hierarchical deterministic (HD) wallets: child keys can be lifted to parent keys, master key to master seed, and master seed to mnemonic phrase bytes.
  - Statements that only involve hash operations (master private key, hardened child key, BIP39 seed) are far cheaper to prove than those requiring secp256k1 elliptic curve operations (public key, non-hardened child key, Ethereum address).
- The main technical challenge was fitting the prover onto hardware wallets with extremely constrained memory (~334K stack+heap on Ledger Flex).
- The solution uses a two-stage architecture:
  - Stage 1: zkBoo (MPC-in-the-head) runs on the secure element with streaming output; linear time in trace length, memory proportional to largest intermediate state.
  - Stage 2: A succinct proof lifter on an untrusted host machine wraps the zkBoo proof for on-chain verification; the host does not need to be trusted since each zkBoo response is independently zero-knowledge.
- Three succinct lifters were implemented: a Stark-based (Plonky3 + FRI) post-quantum lifter, SP1 (not post-quantum), and Flock.
- zkBoo itself never materializes the full circuit; gates are executed as a Rust program, only registers for the largest intermediate state are allocated, and proofs are streamed off-device immediately.

sections.heading: Secure OS Limitations for Master Key and Seed Statements
sections.summary: Proving master seed or mnemonic ownership requires secure OS internals that stock Ledger firmware does not expose; feasibility was demonstrated with mock data.
sections.body:
- Stock Ledger BOLOS does not expose the master entropy or seed phrase bytes to user-space applications, preventing real proofs of compromised master key or seed ownership.
- The team tested these statements with mock pre-images on-device to confirm hardware feasibility; the constraint is purely a secure OS API limitation, not a hardware limitation.
- Accessing these internals would require Ledger firmware integration or a custom secure OS build.
- These proofs are characterized as more relevant for forensic or dispute-resolution scenarios than for on-chain emergency recovery.

sections.heading: On-Device Proving Benchmarks and Constraints
sections.summary: Hardened child key proof takes ~3 hours and ~22 MB on Ledger Flex; elliptic curve statements take days and produce ~1 GB proofs.
sections.body:
- For master private key and hardened child key statements, each response is ~50 KB and takes ~30 seconds on-device; full 438-response proof (128-bit post-quantum soundness) is ~22 MB and takes ~3 hours.
- Elliptic curve ("elephant") statements were optimized 350X since the April presentation but still require several days and produce ~1 GB proofs.
  - The argument for burning the private key instead: in a quantum emergency the private key is worthless anyway, so proving from the private key (cheap) rather than the public key (expensive) is preferable.
- Full BIP39 seed derivation at 2048 PBKDF2 rounds is projected at ~150 days on-device — technically feasible in memory but extremely slow.
- Per-response size for elephant statements dropped from 1 GB (at EthCC) to ~3 MB after summer optimizations — a ~300X improvement.
- Maximum I/O throughput from Ledger Flex measured at ~3 KB/s during proving (theoretical max ~20-25 KB/s without computation load); this throughput ceiling is a dominant bottleneck.
- All statements fit within Ledger Flex memory; 4 factory-reset-level device wipes occurred during memory tuning.
- 438 responses provide 128-bit post-quantum soundness (accounting for Grover); 219 responses suffice for classical 128-bit security.
- Some statements do not fit on the Ledger Nano S Plus due to tighter memory; the hardened child key statement does fit. Further Nano S Plus optimization was deprioritized.

sections.heading: Succinct Proof Lifting and On-Chain Verification
sections.summary: SP1 lift verified on-chain at ~280K gas but is not post-quantum; Flock lift proves in 12 seconds and is most promising but lacks on-chain verification yet.
sections.body:
- SP1 lifter: ~1 hour proving time on a metal fork of the SP1 prover, 356-byte proof, verified on Ethereum L1 at ~280K gas. Not post-quantum.
- Flock lifter: ~12 seconds proving time on multi-threaded CPU, 1.2 MB proof, near-instant off-chain verification. On-chain verification not yet implemented but expected to be the focus going forward.
- Stark lifter (Plonky3 + FRI): post-quantum but extremely expensive on-chain; recursion reduces cost ~10,000X but still far too much gas for L1. Potentially viable on Starknet.
- Both SP1 and Stark lifters use a two-step process: first prove responses and transcript, then aggregate via recursion for succinctness.
- Flock is hash-friendly, which matters because most of the lifting circuit complexity comes from the hash absorptions in the Fiat-Shamir transcript, not the circuit execution itself.
- Off-chain zkBoo verification is very cheap: a few seconds to ~2 minutes for a 1 GB proof, done in constant memory via stream verification.

sections.heading: Remaining Work and Next Steps for Proof of Seed
sections.summary: Key remaining tasks include Flock on-chain verification, batch aggregation for emergency-scale use, and account abstraction integration.
sections.body:
- Account abstraction integration has not been built yet; it is straightforward but conditional on viable on-chain verifiers.
- Batch aggregation of lifted proofs is needed for emergency scenarios involving thousands of accounts; not yet implemented.
- Full 438-response lifting for elephant (ECC) proofs has only been run up to 96 responses (~70-80 hours); full runs are planned.
- Software ("sponsored") provers exist for users without hardware wallets or with more powerful secure elements.
- Bitcoin and Solana statements were implemented and benchmarked but not lifted; not relevant to Ethereum.
- A paper formalizing the cryptographic construction is expected in a few weeks.

sections.heading: Daisugi Testnet and SPHINCS Transaction Demo
sections.summary: Riva Labs demonstrated SPHINCS signing via software wallet, Ledger, and Trezor on the new persistent Daisugi testnet using non-native account abstraction with ERC-4337.
sections.body:
- Antonio Sanso announced that the daisugi.fyi testnet will stay up as the group's testnet from today onward; an earlier testnet was stood up a few months ago and then dismissed. Infrastructure set up by Giulio Rebuffo.
  - Currently uses non-native account abstraction (ERC-4337); signature aggregation with Stark verification is among the experiments planned over the next weeks.
- Riva Labs demonstrated SPHINCS signing using their NiceTry browser extension connected to the testnet, with three signing modes:
  - Software wallet: ~60 ms signing time on a retail computer.
  - Ledger Nano S Plus: ~10-12 seconds, most time spent on I/O and proof verification on-device rather than actual signing.
  - Trezor Safe 3: slightly faster than Ledger due to higher I/O throughput for streaming the proof.
- All three signing paths use the same stock SPHINCS zkSNARK verifier on-chain — the verification is identical regardless of signing device.
- SPHINCS parameters used: budget of 2^20 signatures.
- The signing now includes a pre-compute grinding proof (Groth16 for now): the hardware wallet sends a seed, the host grinds the hypertree on CPU, produces a ~100 KB proof of correct grinding, streams it to the device, which verifies before signing.
  - This proof verification accounts for most of the ~10-second signing time on hardware wallets (up from 1.5 seconds in prior demos without this proof).
- The gas figure shown in the explorer is a rough estimate extrapolated from measurements taken with other parameters, and includes calldata gas as well as verification gas. Giulio is still working on full trace logging; more gas information will be added to the testnet explorer.
- Keygen at 2^20 takes approximately 5-7 seconds depending on hardware.

sections.heading: MPC Signing for SPHINCS
sections.summary: Riva Labs has a working multi-party SPHINCS signing implementation with zero interactive rounds during signing; no paper is published yet.
sections.body:
- Riva Labs confirmed a fully working MPC implementation for SPHINCS signing that uses the same basis as the hardware wallet scheme and goes through the same on-chain verifier.
- The MPC signing process requires zero interactive rounds at signing time.
- The implementation runs on Linux servers with any number of participating devices; it has been tested end-to-end with on-chain submission.
- This is an original design by Riva Labs; no public paper or documentation exists yet.
- In response to a chat question noting that thresholdized SPHINCS was previously thought not to exist: the team confirmed the MPC parties do communicate at every step of key material production and signing, but declined to share further details pending future publication.
